All 11 fringe words are drawn from classic spring themes (weather, nature, animals, plants) that typically appear across spring-themed books in early childhood and SPED classrooms. If this board is paired with a specific spring book (e.g. 'The Tiny Seed' by Eric Carle or 'Fletcher and the Springtime Blossoms'), consider replacing the hero image and adjusting fringe words to match that specific text.

spring_for_sophie.title: Spring for Sophie
spring_for_sophie.author: Yael Werber

hero.description: Young girl (child protagonist) eagerly waiting for and discovering spring — Sophie is a generic child character so a Boardmaker girl image may suffice, but she has a distinctive illustrated style
hero.source_note: Sophie is a generic child character — a Boardmaker 'girl' icon is acceptable; if the classroom edition uses her specific illustrated likeness, source from publisher or TPT

spring_for_sophie.notes: Several fringe words (robin, bud, rain, sun, mud, worm, flower) already exist in activity_images or aac_extras — these can be reused directly. 'Spring' is the central concept and most important fringe word; a seasonal image (flowers, sunshine, green landscape) works best. 'Wait' is a key emotional/action word as Sophie waits impatiently for spring to arrive — it is picturable (child waiting) and highly communicative for this book. 'Grow' and 'butterfly' round out the transformation/nature theme central to the story. Colour words (green, yellow) were considered but 'colour' is already in core row 5, so they were not prioritised over concrete nouns.

spring_is_here.title: Spring Is Here
spring_is_here.author: Will Hillenbrand

hero.name: Mole
hero.description: Small brown mole character, main protagonist who tries to wake Bear to announce spring

ambiguous.issue: Could mean the season or a coiled spring object
ambiguous.reason: Book is about the arrival of the spring season

spring_is_here.notes: Mole and Bear are the two main characters; mole is generic enough for Boardmaker library using 'mole animal' search. Bear is also generic (brown bear hibernating). Key story arc is Mole trying to wake Bear to announce spring — 'wake' is a critical action verb. Trumpet is a key plot object Mole uses. Honey is Bear's motivation to wake. Butterfly signals spring arrival visually. Snow and cave represent winter setting they are leaving. Several of these words (mole, bear, honey, trumpet, rain, sun, flower) already exist in activity_images or aac_extras and can be reused directly.

spring_stinks.notes: Spring Stinks features Bruce the Bear (from the Mother Bruce series) who grumpily endures the sights, smells, and creatures of spring — especially a persistent skunk. The word 'stinky' is central to the book's humour and theme and should be included even though it is slightly abstract; it is picturable (e.g. stink lines symbol). Several vocabulary items (skunk, flower, bee, butterfly, mud, smell, nose, trail) already exist in activity_images or aac_extras and can be reused. 'Spring' as a season may not have a perfect Boardmaker symbol — a sun-with-flowers or sprouting plant image may be the best match. 'Outside' covers the setting of the story. 'Hide' captures Bruce's key reaction/behaviour. Recommend checking existing activity_images assets for skunk, flower, bee, butterfly, mud before sourcing new icons.

stand_tall_molly_lou_melon.title: Stand Tall, Molly Lou Melon

ambiguous.reason: Molly Lou stacks pennies on her buck teeth as a trick in the book

stand_tall_molly_lou_melon.notes: Stand Tall Molly Lou Melon is about self-confidence, embracing differences, and standing up to bullying. Molly Lou is tiny with buck teeth and a bullfrog voice but uses her unique traits as superpowers. Key vocabulary centres on size contrast (small/tall), physical traits (teeth), social themes (bully, friend, brave, proud), and the specific activities Molly Lou excels at (sing, catch, stack). 'Brave' and 'proud' are slightly abstract but are picturable emotions central to the book's message and appropriate for AAC use. 'Grandmother' could be a 12th candidate as Grandma gives Molly Lou her confidence, but 'proud' was prioritised as more communicatively generative.

stone_soup.title: Stone Soup
stone_soup.author: Classic (Traditional Folk Tale)

hero.name: Soldier / Traveller with pot
hero.description: A travelling stranger or soldier carrying a large pot, the central character who tricks the villagers into sharing by making 'stone soup'
hero.source_note: Generic traveller or soldier figure — Boardmaker 'man' or 'soldier' icon acceptable; no named/branded character

ambiguous.issue: Could mean fire (flames under a cooking pot) or fire (danger/emergency)
ambiguous.reason: In Stone Soup, fire is used to heat the pot for cooking — the campfire/cooking fire meaning is correct

ambiguous.issue: Could mean a pebble/rock (noun) or the action 'to stone' (verb)
ambiguous.reason: The story centres on a literal stone/rock dropped into the pot — the noun meaning is correct

stone_soup.notes: Stone Soup is a classic folk tale about community and sharing. Key vocabulary centres on cooking actions (stir, add), food items (carrot, pot, stone, soup), and social concepts (share, together, hungry). 'Villager' represents the townsfolk characters; a generic 'person' or 'people' Boardmaker icon is suitable. The existing activity_images already cover pot, stone, carrot, water, village, spoon, turnip, bread, onion, potato, and aac_extras cover share, cook, stir, hungry — so the fringe selection here prioritises the most story-critical items including 'soup' (the finished product), 'fire' (cooking method), 'together' (the story's moral theme), and 'add' (the repeated action of villagers contributing ingredients). 'Villager' and 'hungry' are prioritised over vegetable duplicates already covered in existing assets.

strictly_no_elephants.title: Strictly No Elephants
strictly_no_elephants.author: Lisa Mantchev

hero.name: Little Elephant
hero.description: Small, round, cute elephant character — the boy's pet elephant from the book cover
hero.source_note: Generic elephant symbol from Boardmaker should work well for this character

ambiguous.issue: Already exists in fixed core row 2 as a core word
ambiguous.reason: The book's central theme is belonging and being included; 'belong' is more book-specific and avoids duplication with core. Swap 'different' for 'belong' in fringe.

strictly_no_elephants.notes: The book's core themes are inclusion, belonging, and friendship — a pet elephant is excluded from Pet Club because he is different, then the boy and his elephant start their own inclusive club. Key vocabulary should reflect these social-emotional themes. 'Different' appears in fixed core row 2 so 'belong' is recommended as a replacement fringe word. The existing activity_images already include 'elephant' which can serve double duty as the hero image. Secondary animal characters (penguin, skunk, bat, whale) are already in activity_images and may be used as supporting fringe if the board is expanded. The 11 chosen words prioritise the book's social narrative over character names.

swimmy.title: Swimmy
swimmy.author: Leo Lionni

hero.name: Swimmy
hero.description: Small black fish among red fish, distinctive Leo Lionni character with eye detail
hero.source_note: Named character — source from Creative Fabrica or TPT clip art; must be black fish distinct from red schoolmates

ambiguous.issue: Could be size adjective or a generic concept card
ambiguous.reason: Used to describe the large tuna that threatens the fish; size adjective meaning is correct

ambiguous.issue: Could map to colour swatch or to a black object/animal

swimmy.notes: Swimmy by Leo Lionni is a story about a small black fish who loses his school to a large tuna, explores the deep ocean alone, and ultimately leads a new school of red fish to swim together in the shape of a giant fish to scare away predators. Key themes are courage, teamwork, and being different. 'Together' is a critical concept word for the climax. 'Scared' and 'hide' support emotional and action vocabulary central to the plot. Red and black are story-critical colours (the red fish vs Swimmy's black). The existing activity_images already include fish, tuna, and ocean which can be reused. 'Tuna' represents the antagonist/danger. Consider adding a secondary 'eye' card if the teacher wants to discuss Swimmy's role as the eye of the big fish formation.

tacky_penguin.author: Helen Lester

hero.name: Tacky the Penguin
hero.description: Odd-bird-out penguin wearing a loud striped shirt and bow tie, distinctive character from cover
hero.source_note: Named distinctive character — source from Creative Fabrica or TPT clip art; must show Tacky in his recognisable colourful shirt

ambiguous.issue: Could mean the month March or the action of marching in a line
ambiguous.reason: In this book the penguins march in a neat line — the action verb is correct

ambiguous.issue: Could be represented as a sound wave icon or a shouting person — abstract adjective
ambiguous.reason: Tacky is described as loud and off-key; a shouting or noisy icon best represents this; confirm Boardmaker has a clear 'loud' adjective image rather than a volume symbol

tacky_penguin.notes: Tacky is the odd-one-out penguin who saves his friends from hunters by being gloriously odd. Key story beats: the orderly companions vs chaotic Tacky, the hunters arriving and being frightened away by Tacky's antics (loud singing, cannonball splashing, wrong-words marching). 'scared' maps best to Boardmaker 'afraid' icon. 'brave' may need checking — try 'brave' or 'strong'. Existing activity_images (striped shirt, bow tie, snowflake) and aac_extras (different, silly, funny, cold) complement this board well and can be used in classroom extension activities without needing fringe slots.

ten_apples_up_on_top.title: Ten Apples Up On Top!
ten_apples_up_on_top.author: Theo LeSieg

hero.name: Lion (Ten Apples Up On Top)
hero.description: Upright cartoon lion balancing apples on his head, Dr. Seuss style illustration by Roy McKie
hero.source_note: Seuss-style lion is distinctive — generic Boardmaker lion won't match cover art; source from TPT or Creative Fabrica with Seuss/LeSieg styling

ambiguous.issue: Could mean the season (autumn) or the action of falling/dropping
ambiguous.reason: In this book the apples tumble off heads — fall as an action/verb is the correct meaning

ambiguous.issue: Could mean a spinning toy (top) or the uppermost position (on top)
ambiguous.reason: The book is about balancing apples on top of heads — positional meaning is correct; search 'above' or 'on top' for a positional symbol

character_images_needed: Lion (Ten Apples Up On Top) — Seuss/LeSieg style
ten_apples_up_on_top.notes: The three main animal characters are lion, tiger, and dog — all central to the story and worth naming individually on the board. 'Bird' appears in the climactic parade/chase scene and is worth including. 'Stack' and 'try' capture the core repetitive actions of the book (stacking apples, trying to balance) and support retelling. 'Ten' is thematically critical as the target number throughout. Core words 'more' and 'again' are already in core rows and do not need fringe slots. The existing activity_images already include apple, ten, count, tiger, dog, lion, balance, and fall — all of these are reused here, reducing new asset creation needed.

ten_black_dots.title: Ten Black Dots
ten_black_dots.author: Donald Crews

hero.name: Black Dot
hero.description: A single bold black circle/dot — the central recurring visual element of the book, simple geometric shape on white background
hero.source_note: Generic black circle — a solid black dot PNG or Boardmaker circle shape will work well

ten_black_dots.notes: Ten Black Dots is a pure counting book — numbers 1–10 are the entire curriculum focus, making them the ideal fringe vocabulary. Each number is shown alongside a real-world object (sun, fox, buttons, etc.) made from that many dots, but the objects rotate page by page and are less consistently salient than the numbers themselves. The hero slot uses 'dot' (a solid black circle) as the iconic recurring element students will associate with the book cover and every page. The colour 'black' is included as the one consistent descriptor throughout. Pre-existing activity_images vocab (dot, hat, moon, sun, fish, flower, snake, button, eye, balloon, wheel, fox) and aac_extras (count, ten, circle, shape) nicely complement this board — consider adding them to a second page or extension board so students can label the dot-objects on each page. Number symbols 1–10 should map directly to Boardmaker numeral PNGs.

the_bad_guys.title: The Bad Guys
the_bad_guys.author: Aaron Blabey

ambiguous.issue: Could mean morally bad (villain) or feeling bad (unwell)
ambiguous.reason: In this book 'bad' refers to the villain identity/reputation of the characters — use the standard Boardmaker 'bad' symbol showing thumbs down or negative expression

ambiguous.issue: Could mean catching a ball (sport) or catching a person/animal (chase/grab)
ambiguous.reason: In this book catching refers to grabbing/capturing characters — use the action catch/grab symbol rather than a sports ball symbol

the_bad_guys.notes: The Bad Guys by Aaron Blabey is a humorous early chapter book about a wolf, shark, piranha, and snake who want to be heroes. Key themes are good vs bad, friendship, helping others, and comedy. 'help' appears in both fixed core row 2 and fringe — consider swapping 'help' in fringe for 'laugh' or 'hero' since help is already a core word. Suggested replacement: swap 'help' for 'hero' to better reflect the book's central theme of the bad guys trying to do good deeds. Secondary characters (Mr. Shark, Mr. Snake, Mr. Piranha) are all named characters but are represented by their animal type words in the fringe rather than sourced images, which is appropriate for this board. The piranha was omitted from the fringe animal list in favour of the more picturable/searchable animals — consider swapping 'spider' for 'piranha' if the teacher prioritises book accuracy over symbol availability.

the_best_nest.title: The Best Nest
the_best_nest.author: P.D. Eastman

hero.name: Mr. Bird
hero.description: Small cheerful bird character from P.D. Eastman's The Best Nest, distinct illustrated style
hero.source_note: Named/distinctive P.D. Eastman character — source from TPT or Creative Fabrica clip art matching book illustration style

ambiguous.reason: In this book, flying refers to Mr. Bird's movement through the air — the verb meaning is correct

ambiguous.reason: Central to the book's theme of finding the best nest — use a Boardmaker symbol showing 1st place or best ribbon if available, otherwise the word card

the_best_nest.notes: The story centres on Mr. Bird and Mrs. Bird searching for the best nest, eventually returning to their original tree nest when Mrs. Bird lays an egg. Key vocabulary supports retelling the journey: nest-building materials (twig, feather), locations (tree, house), and the resolution (egg, baby, best). 'Sing' is included because Mr. Bird sings 'I love my house' — a repeated refrain central to the book. Mrs. Bird could be added as a secondary character image if the board is extended. Existing activity_images (bird, nest, egg, tree, house) and aac_extras (fly, build, feather, twig) overlap well with recommended fringe — reuse those assets where possible.

the_color_monster.title: The Color Monster: A Story About Emotions

ambiguous.reason: In this book mixed up refers to emotions all tangled together — emotional confusion is the correct meaning

ambiguous.reason: The monster sorts emotions into glass jars in the story — the noun container is the correct meaning

the_color_monster.notes: The Color Monster is built entirely around named emotions (happy, sad, angry, scared, calm, love) so all six emotion words are high-priority fringe even though they are abstract — they ARE picturable as faces and are the core vocabulary of the book. The hero image must show the monster in a neutral or multicoloured state so students can point to it without it being anchored to a single emotion. If sourcing multiple hero variants (one per emotion colour) is feasible, that would extend the board's utility but is not required for the base board.

the_day_you_begin.title: The Day You Begin
the_day_you_begin.author: Jacqueline Woodson

hero.name: Angelina (girl from cover)

hero.source_note: Named/distinctive illustrated character — source from Creative Fabrica or TPT clip art matching Rafael López illustration style

ambiguous.reason: In this book 'alone' conveys the feeling of being isolated or left out at school, so the emotional/lonely depiction is correct

ambiguous.issue: Could be pictured as a start button, a starting line, or an abstract arrow — many possible images

character_images_needed: Angelina (girl from cover of The Day You Begin)
the_day_you_begin.notes: This book focuses on themes of belonging, identity, and courage when entering a new environment as an outsider. Key vocabulary prioritises social-emotional words (brave, alone, welcome, begin) alongside relationship nouns (friend, family) and the core setting (school). 'Summer' is included because children in the story share — or notably do not share — experiences of summer holidays, making it a key story discussion point. Several words (brave, different, friend, share) already exist in aac_extras and (school) in activity_images, so no new sourcing is needed for those. The hero image will require custom sourcing to match Rafael López's distinctive illustration style, as a generic Boardmaker child icon will not be recognisable to students familiar with the book cover.

the_garden_that_we_grew.title: The Garden That We Grew
the_garden_that_we_grew.author: Joan Holub

hero.name: Pumpkin (giant pumpkin)
hero.description: Large round orange pumpkin, the central growing object of the story — children plant a seed and grow a giant pumpkin
hero.source_note: Generic pumpkin icon available in Boardmaker library

ambiguous.issue: Could mean to choose (verb) or to harvest/pull from plant (verb)
ambiguous.reason: Book is about harvesting a pumpkin from the garden; harvesting meaning is correct

ambiguous.issue: Could mean the planet Earth or soil/dirt
ambiguous.reason: Book context is gardening; soil/dirt meaning is correct — use 'dirt' or 'soil' search term

the_garden_that_we_grew.notes: This rhyming picture book follows a group of children planting a pumpkin seed through to harvest. The pumpkin itself is the most recognisable central object and makes a strong hero icon — it is already in the existing activity_images vocab which is ideal. Several existing vocab items (seed, vine) are reused from the existing library. 'Water' here refers to the action of watering plants, not water as a drink — the icon_search_term 'water plant' clarifies this. 'Big' is included because the pumpkin growing to giant size is a core narrative payoff students will want to comment on. 'Orange' is included as a colour because naming the pumpkin's colour is a key concrete communication opportunity. 'Earth/dirt' replaces a more abstract word to keep vocabulary concrete and picturable.

the_gas_we_pass.title: The Gas We Pass: The Story of Farts
the_gas_we_pass.author: Shinta Cho

hero.name: Generic child character

hero.source_note: Generic child figure — standard Boardmaker child symbol is suitable

the_gas_we_pass.notes: This nonfiction picture book explains digestion and flatulence in simple terms. Most key vocabulary already exists in activity_images and aac_extras (body, stomach, burp, food, beans, tummy, laugh, fart, funny). Priority fringe words focus on the digestive process and sensory/social aspects of the topic. The word 'gas' is central to the title and concept. 'Animal' is useful as the book compares human and animal flatulence. Avoid 'laugh' as a fringe word since the core row already covers emotional reactions adequately; 'funny' is retained as it is more concrete and picturable. The book has no named character so a generic child symbol suffices for the hero slot.

the_giving_tree.notes: The Giving Tree by Shel Silverstein follows a boy and a tree across a lifetime. Key vocabulary reflects the objects the tree gives (apples, branches for a house, trunk for a boat) and the emotional arc (happy, give). The tree itself is the hero and needs custom sourcing as its illustrated face is distinctive. 'Old' is included because the passage of time and the boy ageing is central to the story. 'Money' is included because the boy sells apples for money in middle story stages. All 11 fringe words are concrete and picturable.

hero.source_note: Generic bunny rabbit — Boardmaker library should have a suitable match

ambiguous.reason: The story is about a duckling hatching from the golden egg — the animal meaning is correct

ambiguous.reason: The egg is described as golden — a gold/yellow colour swatch is the most picturable representation

the_golden_egg_book.notes: The Golden Egg Book centres on a lonely bunny who finds a mysterious golden egg and eventually meets the duckling that hatches from it — themes of curiosity, loneliness, waiting, and friendship are central. 'Sleep' and 'wake' are already noted in aac_extras and are highly relevant as the bunny falls asleep waiting for the egg to hatch. 'Hatch' is also in aac_extras. 'Golden' is best represented by a gold colour swatch since Boardmaker is unlikely to have a book-specific golden egg icon. 'Pond' is the key setting. 'Alone' captures the emotional core of the story and is concrete enough to picture. The hero bunny is generic enough for Boardmaker's standard rabbit/bunny icon to suffice. If the existing activity_images already include bunny, egg, bird, friend, these can be reused directly on the board.

the_great_eggscape.notes: The Great Eggscape! is an Easter-themed adventure where egg characters hide and are found. Key vocabulary focuses on the hunt/escape narrative: hiding, finding, running, and feeling emotions (scared, happy). 'Yolk' is included as a book-specific concrete noun central to egg identity in the story. Several words (egg, basket, hide, find) already exist in activity_images and aac_extras from prior use, which is ideal for reuse. 'Nest' is included as a story setting element. Core words 'more', 'stop', 'go', and 'finished' already on the fixed core rows cover additional narrative moments. Consider pairing this board with an Easter egg hunt activity for generalisation.

The existing activity_images vocab covers most key tools (hammer, saw, wrench, drill, ladder, tape_measure, pliers, hard_hat) and aac_extras cover build, fix, worker, job — all reusable here. 'tool' (generic) is added as a unifying concept word. 'pliers' and 'job' from existing assets were deprioritised in favour of 'tool' and 'ladder' for broader communicative utility on the board, but could substitute if preferred. The hero is a generic construction worker so no custom sourcing is needed.

ambiguous.reason: In this book, stomach refers to the physical feeling of worry in the stomach (butterflies/knots); body part image is correct

wilma_jean_worry_machine.notes: This book by Julia Cook addresses anxiety and worry in children. Key vocabulary centres on emotions (worry, scared, calm), body sensations (stomach, breathe), and the central metaphor of a 'worry machine' (machine, brain). The existing activity_images already include machine, school, stomach, and backpack which can be reused. 'Better' and 'try' are important as the book ends with coping strategies and reassurance. 'Breathe' is a core coping skill modelled in the book and highly useful for AAC users to communicate during anxious moments.

wonder.author: R.J. Palacio

wonder.notes: Wonder by R.J. Palacio is a middle-grade novel about Auggie Pullman, a boy with Treacher Collins syndrome starting mainstream school for the first time. Core themes are kindness, belonging, facial difference, bullying, and friendship. For younger or lower-verbal SPED users, the picture book adaptation 'We're All Wonders' (also by Palacio) may be a better classroom match and would share most of this vocabulary. The word 'different' appears in the fixed core row — teachers may wish to swap it for 'unique' or 'stand out' in the fringe to avoid redundancy. The astronaut helmet is the most iconic visual symbol for Auggie and should be prioritised when sourcing his character image.

wonky_donkey.notes: The Wonky Donkey is a cumulative song-book where each page adds a new descriptor for the donkey (wonky, stinky, dinky, etc.). Core vocabulary like 'same', 'more', and 'different' on the fixed rows are especially useful here given the repetitive cumulative structure. The existing activity_images vocab (donkey, song, sunglasses, hat, leg, hoof, tail, ear, eye) and aac_extras (silly, funny, cool, groovy) cover most fringe needs well — only 'smell' is a new addition. 'eye' from existing images is relevant since the donkey has only one eye but was replaced in fringe by 'smell' as more communicatively functional. Consider adding 'eye' as an optional swap if students want to discuss the one-eye feature specifically.

worm_weather.notes: This board covers both Worm Weather (Jean Taft) and Compost Stew (Mary McKenna Siddals), which are frequently paired in classroom garden units. Core vocabulary like rain, mud, soil, and compost covers both books. Wiggle and crawl are high-value action words for worm movement. Rain boots was deliberately excluded as it is already in existing activity_images and is not a communication priority; recycle and food waste from aac_extras were also deprioritised in favour of more concrete story-action words. If only one book is being read, consider swapping crawl for rain boots or recycle depending on which title is in use.
